artworks.title: Sisyphus
artworks.description: One of Titian's underworld Furias for Mary of Hungary: Sisyphus strains beneath the boulder he must forever drive uphill, cliffs and infernal fire closing around him. Oil on canvas, Museo del Prado, Madrid — the Corinthian king's punishment as a colossal single figure of futile labour.

artworks.title: Sisyphus
artworks.description: The Venetian Baroque painter crowds the eternal sentence into a dark, muscular canvas: Sisyphus locked against the rock that will always roll back down. Oil on canvas in the Mauritshuis, The Hague (inv. 335) — the crafty king of Corinth reduced to raw, repeating effort.

artworks.title: Sisyphus
artworks.description: Stuck's Symbolist Sisyphus bends naked into the stone, the hillside a stark plane of struggle without landscape comfort. Painted in 1920, the image became one of the modern emblems of the absurd labour Camus would later name — the boulder as destiny.

films.title: Triangle
films.description: Smith's time-loop horror restages the Corinthian king's punishment as a yacht that cannot leave its own wake — Sisyphus rewritten as a mother trapped in a repeating day of violence.

popCulture.title: The Myth of Sisyphus
popCulture.creator: Albert Camus
popCulture.description: Camus' essay makes the rolling stone the emblem of the absurd — and ends by imagining Sisyphus happy, turning the underworld labour into modern philosophy's most famous image of defiance.

popCulture.title: Sisyphean
popCulture.description: English borrowed the king's name for any endless, futile labour — a daily word that keeps the Corinthian punishment alive long after the underworld scene is forgotten.

popCulture.title: Hades
popCulture.creator: Supergiant Games
popCulture.description: Supergiant's underworld roguelike keeps Sisyphus as a cheerful boulder-pusher in Tartarus — the eternal sentence turned into a warm, talkative side character.
